justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift assumption across all three horizons, starting near what I would have assessed as the prevailing market level around 1018 for the one-day horizon, rising slightly to 1022 at one week and 1035 at one month. The gentle upward slope in the point estimates embeds a small positive drift consistent with a risk-premium assumption — essentially, that over time equities or whatever underlying asset this tracks tends to appreciate slightly above its current level. The incremental increases are small because I was not incorporating any strong directional catalyst; rather, the base case assumed continuation of recent conditions with no dramatic regime shift.

The confidence interval widths widen appropriately as the horizon extends, reflecting the well-established statistical reality that uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 56 points, which reflects typical short-term volatility — essentially daily price noise. By one week, that expands to about 105 points, and at one month the interval covers 210 points, capturing the accumulation of daily randomness as well as the increased probability that a meaningful macro event, earnings release, central bank decision, or geopolitical development could materially shift the price level. The ratio of widths across horizons is roughly consistent with a square-root-of-time scaling, which is the standard assumption under geometric Brownian motion.

Several specific risks could push realized outcomes outside the stated intervals. On the upside, an unexpected positive catalyst — a stronger-than-anticipated economic data release, a dovish surprise from a central bank, or a significant geopolitical de-escalation — could drive prices well above the upper bounds, particularly at the monthly horizon. On the downside, a sudden liquidity shock, an unexpected hawkish policy pivot, a credit event, or an escalation in geopolitical tensions could push prices sharply below the lower bounds. Fat tails in financial return distributions mean that extreme outcomes occur more frequently than a normal distribution would imply, so the stated 90% intervals should be understood as approximate guides rather than hard limits.

It is also worth acknowledging model uncertainty itself as a source of risk. The intervals were constructed under assumptions about volatility and drift that may not hold if the underlying volatility regime shifts — for instance, if implied volatility spikes due to an options market repricing or if correlations across assets break down. In that sense, the one-month interval in particular should be treated with some humility, as a month is long enough for the fundamental character of the market environment to change in ways that were not foreseeable at the time the forecast was made.
